questions.text: In a competitive firm with several inputs and outputs, economic profit equals what?

options.a: Revenue from outputs minus the opportunity cost of all inputs.
options.b: Revenue minus only cash payments to workers.
options.c: The difference between output quantities and input quantities.
options.d: Revenue minus sunk historical expenditures regardless of opportunity cost.

questions.text: Why should the owner's time be counted as a cost in economic-profit calculations?

options.a: It is never used in production.
options.b: It is necessarily a fixed accounting expense.
options.c: It has an opportunity cost even if no wage is explicitly paid.
options.d: It has a price equal to zero.

questions.text: Why should machinery already owned by a firm be assigned a rental cost in economic profit?

options.a: The firm forgoes the market rental return it could earn elsewhere.
options.b: Capital costs matter only if paid in cash this year.
options.c: Historical purchase price is always the current opportunity cost.
options.d: The machinery cannot be used in other industries.

questions.text: What is a fixed input in the short run?

options.a: An input whose quantity cannot be adjusted over that horizon.
options.b: An input with a permanently zero price.
options.c: An input whose marginal product is always zero.
options.d: An input that cannot be employed in the long run.

questions.text: What is a variable input?

options.a: An input that always makes profit positive.
options.b: An input whose quantity the firm can adjust over the relevant horizon.
options.c: An input that has a fixed total cost regardless of quantity.
options.d: An input supplied only by monopoly.

questions.text: What is a quasi-fixed input?

options.a: An input needed in equal quantity for every additional unit of output.
options.b: An input that is free and infinitely available.
options.c: An input whose price rises with output by definition.
options.d: An input required in a fixed amount whenever output is positive, but not necessarily when output is zero.

questions.text: Why can a competitive firm rationally have negative economic profit in the short run?

options.a: Marginal revenue must be below zero in competition.
options.b: Some unavoidable fixed costs may remain even when output is zero.
options.c: Competitive firms cannot shut down production.
options.d: Output prices are always below variable costs.

questions.text: Why can long-run optimal profit be at least zero if exit is possible without avoidable commitments?

options.a: All variable inputs become free.
options.b: The firm can set any market price.
options.c: The firm can choose to cease operations rather than incur negative economic profit.
options.d: The firm always earns strictly positive economic profit.

questions.text: For a price-taking firm with output price p and variable input 1 paid w1, what interior first-order condition maximizes short-run profit?

options.a: p equals the marginal product divided by w1.
options.b: Marginal product of input 1 equals p times w1.
options.c: p times the marginal product of input 1 equals w1.
options.d: Total output equals total cost.

questions.text: What is the value of the marginal product of labor for a competitive output market?

options.a: The sales price minus the wage.
options.b: Output price times the marginal physical product of labor.
options.c: The derivative of revenue with respect to output price.
options.d: Wage times the firm's total output.

questions.text: If the value of a variable input's marginal product exceeds its wage, what action can raise profit at an interior choice?

options.a: Stop production regardless of fixed costs.
options.b: Decrease use of that input.
options.c: Increase use of that input.
options.d: Raise input price unilaterally.

questions.text: If the value of a variable input's marginal product is below its wage, what action tends to raise profit?

options.a: Increase the fixed input's price.
options.b: Increase use of that input.
options.c: Increase output price in a competitive market.
options.d: Reduce use of that input.

questions.text: What does an isoprofit line in a one-variable-input production diagram show?

options.a: Consumption bundles yielding the same utility.
options.b: Input-output combinations yielding the same economic profit.
options.c: Input bundles producing the same output.
options.d: Every feasible price vector.

questions.text: In a diagram with output on the vertical axis and a variable input on the horizontal axis, what is the slope of an isoprofit line?

options.a: p/w1.
options.c: The input's marginal product squared.
options.d: w1/p.

questions.text: How does a higher wage for the variable factor change the isoprofit-line slope, holding output price fixed?

options.a: It makes the line steeper.
options.b: It has no effect on slope.
options.c: It makes the line flatter.
options.d: It reverses the slope's sign.

questions.text: What is the geometry of short-run profit maximization for a differentiable concave production function?

options.a: The highest feasible isoprofit line is tangent to the production function.
options.b: The output price equals the marginal product.
options.c: The optimum must always be a corner at zero input.
options.d: The lowest isoprofit line is tangent to the production function.

questions.text: If the wage of a fixed input rises while its quantity cannot change and the firm still operates, what happens to optimal variable-input use in the simple model?

options.a: It changes because the variable input's marginal product instantly doubles.
options.b: It always falls to zero.
options.c: It always increases.
options.d: It is unchanged, although profit falls.

questions.text: If the price of output rises, what generally happens to demand for a variable input with diminishing marginal product?

options.a: It necessarily decreases.
options.b: It remains constant for any technology.
options.c: It increases.
options.d: It becomes negative.

questions.text: If the price of a variable input increases, what generally happens to its short-run profit-maximizing demand?

options.a: It is unaffected because factor demand is vertical.
options.b: It decreases or stays unchanged, holding other conditions fixed.
options.c: It causes output price to rise automatically for a price taker.
options.d: It rises without exception.

questions.text: What determines the short-run supply response of a competitive firm to an increase in output price?

options.a: Higher output value raises the incentive to employ productive variable inputs.
options.b: The market price is set directly by the firm.
options.c: Marginal productivity must rise as employment expands.
options.d: Fixed factors become instantly variable.

questions.text: In long-run profit maximization, what can the firm adjust?

options.a: Only labor, never capital.
options.b: Only fixed costs already sunk.
options.c: All relevant input quantities.
options.d: Only the market price.

questions.text: What condition holds for each freely chosen input in an interior competitive long-run optimum?

options.a: p times its marginal product equals its input price.
options.b: Its marginal product equals total profit.
options.c: Every input quantity equals its market price.
options.d: All marginal products are identical regardless of wages.

questions.text: How does a profit-maximizing factor demand differ from a conditional factor demand?

options.a: Profit-maximizing demand ignores output price.
options.b: Conditional demand maximizes monopoly profit.
options.c: Both are defined by fixed output only.
options.d: Profit-maximizing demand chooses inputs with output endogenous, while conditional demand minimizes input cost for fixed output.

questions.text: What is an inverse factor demand curve?

options.a: The factor price consistent with hiring a given quantity at the optimizing condition.
options.b: The maximum wage that workers are willing to accept.
options.c: The total amount spent on all inputs.
options.d: Market output price as a function of total consumption.

questions.text: Why is the inverse factor demand curve often downward sloping?

options.a: Input supply must be vertical.
options.b: Diminishing marginal product reduces the value of additional units of a factor.
options.c: Output demand must be perfectly inelastic.
options.d: Higher wages always increase physical marginal productivity.

questions.text: For a Cobb-Douglas producer f=x1^a x2^b, what is the factor-1 expenditure at an interior competitive optimum?

options.a: w1 x1 = a p y.
options.b: w1 x1 = b p y.
options.c: w1 x1 = (a+b) p.
options.d: w1 x1 = p/y.

questions.text: For the same Cobb-Douglas producer, what is factor-2 expenditure at an interior competitive optimum?

options.a: w2 x2 = p/x2.
options.b: w2 x2 = (1-a-b) p y.
options.c: w2 x2 = b p y.
options.d: w2 x2 = a p y.

questions.text: For a Cobb-Douglas firm with positive a and b and a+b<1, what kind of returns to scale make a finite interior profit maximum possible under positive prices?

options.a: A production function homogeneous of degree greater than one.
options.b: Decreasing returns to scale.
options.c: Increasing returns to scale.
options.d: Constant returns to scale with strictly positive profit.

questions.text: What is the implication of constant returns to scale and price-taking behavior for long-run economic profit in equilibrium with finite optimal production?

options.a: Economic profit equals the market price.
options.b: Economic profit must be strictly negative.
options.c: Economic profit is zero.
options.d: Economic profit must be strictly positive.

questions.text: Why would positive economic profit be inconsistent with a finite profit maximum under constant returns to scale and unchanged prices?

options.a: Costs would be fixed while output increases.
options.b: Proportionally scaling inputs and output would proportionally increase positive profit without bound.
options.c: Doubling inputs would necessarily reduce output.
options.d: Increasing output necessarily raises output price.

questions.text: If a firm with constant returns to scale can earn positive profit at some scale at given prices, what happens in the idealized model without constraints?

options.a: The firm can increase profit without bound by scaling up.
options.b: Marginal cost always rises to infinity.
options.c: Profit necessarily becomes zero at the next unit.
options.d: The firm must instantly shut down.

questions.text: If output price is below minimum achievable unit cost under constant returns to scale, what is the profit-maximizing supply?

options.a: The firm's initial output regardless of costs.
options.b: Exactly one unit.
options.c: Infinite output.
options.d: Zero.

questions.text: If output price exactly equals constant long-run average cost under constant returns to scale, what happens to profit at feasible scales?

options.a: Profit rises proportionally with output.
options.b: Profit falls proportionally with output.
options.c: Marginal revenue becomes negative.
options.d: Economic profit is zero.

questions.text: What does the envelope theorem imply about the profit function's derivative with respect to output price, under standard differentiability conditions?

options.a: It equals optimal wage payments.
options.b: It equals the marginal product of the fixed input.
options.c: It is always zero.
options.d: It equals the optimal output quantity.

questions.text: Under the same conditions, what is the derivative of maximal profit with respect to an input price?

options.a: The optimal output level.
options.b: The marginal revenue.
options.c: The optimal demand for that input with a positive sign.
options.d: The negative of the optimal demand for that input.

questions.text: Why does an increase in a fixed input's rental rate reduce profit but not necessarily short-run output?

options.a: The fixed input's quantity becomes negative.
options.b: It adds an unavoidable cost without changing the marginal return to the variable input.
options.c: It always changes market demand.
options.d: It increases the marginal physical product of labor.

questions.text: What is the core objective of a competitive firm's profit-maximization problem?

options.a: Maximize gross revenue without regard to costs.
options.b: Minimize average variable cost regardless of the output price.
options.c: Choose feasible output and inputs to maximize revenue minus opportunity cost.
options.d: Maximize the wage bill paid to labor.

questions.text: Which condition is necessary but not always sufficient for a global optimum in a nonlinear profit problem?

options.a: Total revenue must equal zero.
options.b: First-order marginal value equals marginal factor cost at an interior candidate.
options.c: Wage must equal output price at every optimum.
options.d: Average fixed cost must be increasing.

questions.text: Why does a diminishing marginal product help ensure a stable interior optimum when only one variable input is chosen?

options.a: It makes profit strictly linear in input.
options.b: The marginal value product falls as input use rises, so it can cross a constant wage from above.
options.c: It means all factors are perfect substitutes.
options.d: It causes marginal value product to rise without bound.

questions.text: If a firm is a price taker in its factor markets, what is the marginal cost of hiring one additional unit of a particular input?

options.a: The market demand elasticity.
options.b: The firm's output price.
options.c: The given input price.
options.d: Total wage expense paid to all current workers.

questions.text: How should forgone interest on owner-supplied capital be treated when computing economic profit?

options.a: Ignored because it is not a cash transaction.
options.b: Added to revenue.
options.c: Classified as consumer surplus.
options.d: As an opportunity cost of capital.

questions.text: Why is the illustrated profit-maximizing input choice at a tangency?

options.a: Marginal product equals the isoprofit-line slope w1/p.
options.b: The production function and isoprofit line always coincide everywhere.
options.c: The firm's variable-input wage equals zero.
options.d: Marginal product must equal the total cost.
